Variants.Content: Edinburgh Castle sat on a precipitous volcanic crag that dominated Lothian and the southern shore of the Firth of Forth. Within its walls the Scottish royal court, its records, and its treasury could be kept safe, and its craggy approaches commanded views for miles over water and farmland. Its steep slopes gave attackers little firm ground on which to stand siege engines, so assaults on the rock were costly even when the defenders were few. The castle was a symbol as well as a stronghold, because whoever held it held the seat from which royal justice and taxes flowed across the kingdom.

Natural cliff walls and deep wells cut into the rock made the fortress nearly impregnable, so a garrison on the crag could hold out through a long siege. Alexander III's centralized crown governance rested on that security. A lord who wanted to challenge the king knew the castle guard would not open its gates to a rival, and the treasury behind those walls paid the soldiers who kept the peace.
